questions.prompt: Which of these is a colloid?
questions.explain: Milk has fat droplets dispersed in water: an emulsion colloid.

questions.prompt: A mixture shows the Tyndall effect but doesn’t settle and passes through filter paper. It is a…
questions.explain: Scatters light (not a solution) but doesn’t settle or filter (not a suspension).

questions.prompt: Which mixture’s particles can be separated by filtration?
questions.explain: Only suspension particles are big enough to be trapped by filter paper.

questions.prompt: Copper sulfate solution is blue. Is it a solution?
options: No: it must be a suspension
Yes: it is clear and doesn’t scatter light, even though it is coloured
questions.explain: Clear, not cloudy, is what matters. Solutions can be coloured.

items.label: Lemon juice in water with sugar

questions.explain: Clear and stable: solution. Scatters light but stable: colloid. Settles: suspension.

questions.prompt: Match each colloid to its type.
questions.explain: The name depends on the dispersed phase and the dispersion medium.

questions.prompt: Why can you see the headlight beams of a car on a foggy night?
options: Water droplets in the fog scatter the light
questions.explain: Fog is a colloid; its droplets scatter light (Tyndall effect).

questions.prompt: Describe three tests you could use to decide whether a cloudy liquid is a colloid or a suspension, and the result you would expect for each.
questions.modelAnswer: Leave it to stand: a suspension settles, a colloid doesn’t. Filter it: a suspension leaves a residue on the filter paper; a colloid passes through. Look at it closely or under a lens: suspension particles may be visible; colloid particles are not. (A torch beam shows up in both, so it can’t tell them apart, but it does rule out a solution.)
rubric: A third valid test with result
